title: SOLID Principles
summary: Five rules for object-oriented code that survives change. Learn SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP with quick violation-vs-fix examples.

blocks.markdown:
**SOLID** is five design principles that keep object-oriented code easy to change without breaking it.

- **S**RP — Single Responsibility: one reason to change.
- **O**CP — Open/Closed: open to extension, closed to modification.
- **L**SP — Liskov Substitution: subtypes must be substitutable for their base type.
- **I**SP — Interface Segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one.
- **D**IP — Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete details.

Coined by Robert C. Martin; heavily asked in every LLD interview.

blocks.subTitle: Why it matters
blocks.markdown:
Each letter fixes a specific way code rots as it grows.

| Principle | Problem it prevents |
|---|---|
| SRP | Classes that do too much |
| OCP | Editing stable code for every new case |
| LSP | Subclasses that break callers |
| ISP | Forcing unused methods on implementers |
| DIP | High-level code tied to low-level details |

None of these are laws — they're smells to notice, not rules to force everywhere.

**SRP: a class should have one reason to change** — one job, one owner.

- "Responsibility" means an **axis of change**, not a single method. A class can have many methods and still be SRP-compliant if they all serve one purpose.
- Mixing jobs (e.g. business logic + persistence) means a change to one drags in the other, and unrelated features start colliding in the same file.
- Fix by **splitting along each reason to change**, then wiring the pieces together.

blocks.subTitle: Violation vs fix

blocks.markdown:
**OCP: software entities should be open for extension, closed for modification.**

- Add new behavior by **adding new code** (a new subclass or implementation), not by editing tested, working code.
- The usual mechanism is **polymorphism** or plug-in style design: define an abstraction once, add new cases behind it.
- The giveaway violation is a growing `if/else` or `switch` on a type that gets a new branch every time a new case appears.

blocks.subTitle: Violation vs fix

blocks.markdown:
**LSP: a subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is expected, without breaking correctness.**

- If code works with a `Bird`, it must keep working when handed any subclass of `Bird` — same expectations, same guarantees.
- Violations show up as **surprise exceptions**, silently ignored calls, or a subclass that weakens what the base type promised.
- The classic trap: modeling **is-a** relationships from the real world too literally, when behavior doesn't actually match.

blocks.subTitle: Violation vs fix

blocks.markdown:
**ISP: clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use.**

- Prefer **several small, focused interfaces** over one large interface that bundles unrelated capabilities.
- A "fat" interface forces every implementer to stub out or throw on methods that don't apply to them.
- Split by **client need**: group methods by who actually calls them, not by what feels tidy to the author.
- See [interfaces-vs-abstract-classes](interfaces-vs-abstract-classes) for the interface-vs-class tradeoff itself.

blocks.subTitle: Violation vs fix

blocks.markdown:
**DIP: high-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level modules — both should depend on abstractions.**

- "High-level" is policy (business logic); "low-level" is detail (a specific database, API, file format).
- Without DIP, business logic hard-codes a concrete class, so swapping that detail means editing the business logic too.
- With DIP, the high-level code depends on an **interface**; the concrete detail is plugged in from outside.
- This is the principle **behind** [dependency-injection](dependency-injection) — DIP is the design goal, DI is one common technique to achieve it.

blocks.subTitle: Violation vs fix

blocks.markdown:
Common misreadings of SOLID:

- **"Apply all five everywhere."** Over-applying SRP or OCP creates tiny classes and premature abstractions — a maintenance cost of its own. See [coupling-cohesion](coupling-cohesion).
- **"LSP is just about types compiling."** It's about **behavior** — a subtype that type-checks can still violate LSP.
- **"ISP means one method per interface."** It means grouping by client need, not maximum fragmentation.
- **"DIP means always use a DI framework."** DIP is the abstraction dependency; a framework is optional plumbing, not a requirement.

blocks.subTitle: The five letters
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What does each letter in SOLID stand for?**

**S**ingle Responsibility, **O**pen/Closed, **L**iskov Substitution, **I**nterface Segregation, **D**ependency Inversion — five principles for maintainable, extensible OO design, coined by Robert C. Martin.

Interviewers often just want the expansion first, then one line on each if asked to go deeper.

blocks.subTitle: SRP with an example
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain SRP with an example.**

A class should have **one reason to change**. Classic example: an `Invoice` class that both calculates totals and saves itself to a database has two reasons to change — a pricing rule update and a storage change. Split it into `Invoice` (pricing) and `InvoiceRepository` (persistence) so each changes independently.

blocks.subTitle: OCP and LSP together
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain OCP and LSP with an example.**

**OCP**: add a new payment type by adding a new class implementing `PaymentMethod`, not by editing an `if/else` chain. **LSP**: whatever you add must be substitutable — if `PaymentMethod.charge()` is expected to return a confirmation, a new implementation that throws instead breaks every caller silently relying on that contract.

blocks.subTitle: ISP and DIP with an example
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Explain ISP and DIP with an example.**

**ISP**: split a fat `Worker` interface (`work()` + `eat()`) so a `Robot` isn't forced to implement `eat()`. **DIP**: have `OrderService` depend on a `Database` interface instead of a concrete `MySqlDatabase`, so swapping storage doesn't touch business logic.

blocks.subTitle: A common LSP violation
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Give a common real LSP violation.**

`Square extends Rectangle`. Real-world geometry says a square is a rectangle, but if `Rectangle` exposes independent `setWidth`/`setHeight`, `Square` must couple them to stay a square — breaking any caller that resizes width and height separately and expects the area to match. Fix: don't force the inheritance; model both behind a `Shape` interface instead.

blocks.subTitle: DIP vs Dependency Injection
blocks.markdown:
**Q: DIP vs Dependency Injection — same thing?**

No. **DIP** is the design principle: depend on abstractions, not concrete details. **Dependency Injection (DI)** is a technique that supplies those abstractions from outside (constructor, setter, or a DI container) instead of the class creating them itself. DI is how you typically *achieve* DIP, but DIP doesn't require any particular injection mechanism. See [dependency-injection](dependency-injection).
